ann_1.text: This part of the model, which reads only a2, barely changes the predictions.

ann_10.text: The model as a whole clearly predicts 'yes' when exactly two of the six attributes take their first value, and 'no' when none, one, or three or more do.
This holds for every training case at every count, among them 113 with exactly two, and for all 87 test cases.
On average the predicted probability of 'yes' is about 4% for training cases at the counts predicted 'no' and about 82% for cases with exactly two.
For the typical case, moving a4 from 2 to 3 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes', but it stays below 1%.

ann_11.text: This part of the model, which reads a2 and a4, barely changes the predictions.

ann_8.text: This part of the model acts on 143 of the 345 training cases, and none of those 143 cases is actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on, which has every attribute at its first value, this part clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.

For the typical case with a3 = 2, moving a5 away from its first value through this part clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 84%, while with a3 = 1 it stays below 1%.
For the typical case with a6 = 2, moving a3 from 1 to 2 through this part clearly raises it from below 1% to about 75%, while with a6 = 1 it stays below 1%.

Through this part, moving a1, a3, a5 or a6 away from its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' (for the typical case, a3 = 2 takes it from below 1% to about 1%), and giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly lowers it.
Two further combinations, a3 with a2 and a4 with a3, change the predicted probability only slightly, staying below 1% for the typical case.

ann_9.text: Through this part, a2 or a4 taking its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes', and a3, a5 or a6 moving away from its first value slightly lowers it, with the typical case staying below 1% throughout.
Moving a1 from 1 to 2 or to 3 also slightly lowers it (on the training data only).
Moving a4 from 2 to 3 slightly raises it as well, so this part does not treat the two other values of a4 alike.

ann_1.original: An inert unit. The node computes ReLU(0.443 * z(a2:3) - 1.118), and z(a2:3) takes only two values (approximately -0.72 and +1.39), giving maximum pre-activation approximately -0.50 < 0. The unit therefore outputs exactly zero on every input in the domain, and its -2.87 readout to the output contributes nothing. Structurally present, functionally absent: unearned structure that survived selection because nothing priced it.
ann_1.proposed: This part barely changes the predictions.

ann_10.original: The output composes the three children additively under a final ReLU: score = ReLU(2.716 + Ramp - 7.339*Gate - 2.874*Inert), with Inert identically zero. The ramp crosses the decision boundary between one and two active rule indicators, forming the lower edge of a response peak; when a third indicator activates, the gate fires and its -7.34-weighted readout overwhelms the ramp's rise, forming the upper edge. The model therefore scores positive exactly when two of the six indicators are active: a peak at count two realised by one linear ramp plus a single at-least-three gate under the output threshold - more parsimonious than the textbook two-gate bump construction. Extensionally equal to the MONK-2 rule (exactly two of {a1=1..a6=1}) on all 432 possible inputs.
ann_10.proposed: The model predicts 'yes' exactly when two of the six attributes take their first value, and 'no' at every other count, on every training and test case.

ann_11.original: Feature exclusion by elimination. Inputs a2:2 and a4:3 carry no enabled connections: deletion mutations severed them and selection never restored them. The model provably does not consult these features - their values cannot influence any node. For the MONK-2 rule both are redundant given their siblings: a2:2 is implied by a2:1 and a2:3 under one-hot encoding, and a4:3 by a4:1 and a4:2.
ann_11.proposed: This part, which reads a2 and a4, barely changes the predictions.

ann_8.original: An at-least-three-of-six detector. The unit aggregates the six MONK-2 rule indicators (attribute takes its first value): a1:1, a2:1, a4:1, a5:1 enter directly with positive weights; the binary attributes a3 and a6 enter via their complements a3:2, a6:2 with strongly negative weights, which is the same signal inverted. In indicator terms the pre-activation is a near-uniform weighted count (per-indicator coefficients 4.49 to 7.07) minus 14.86: the largest possible two-indicator sum leaves it at -1.82 (off), the smallest possible three-indicator sum reaches +1.26 (on). The unit therefore fires if and only if at least three of the six rule indicators are active, over all 64 indicator patterns.
ann_8.proposed: This part acts on 143 training cases, none of them actually 'yes', and pushes their predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%; through it, moving a further attribute away from its first value raises the predicted probability of 'yes' (a5 when a3 = 2, a3 when a6 = 2).

ann_9.original: A linear count ramp. Evaluated per attribute, the direct connections contribute a positive amount when the attribute takes its first value (a1 +2.56, a2 +2.73, a3 +1.93, a4 +1.69, a5 +2.63, a6 +1.91) and a negative amount otherwise (between -0.02 and -2.03, with small within-attribute variation, e.g. a1=2 vs a1=3 differ by 0.18). The sum therefore rises approximately linearly with the number of active rule indicators; together with the output bias, it crosses zero between one and two active indicators, forming the lower edge of the model's response peak.
ann_9.proposed: This part slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for each attribute at its first value and slightly lowers it for each attribute away from it; it also separates a4 = 3 from a4 = 2.

summary.text: The model clearly predicts 'yes' when exactly two of the six attributes take their first value (a1 = 1, a2 = 1 and so on), and 'no' at every other count: all 113 training cases with exactly two get 'yes', and none of the other training cases do.
It does the same on all 87 test cases, and on average the predicted probability of 'yes' is about 4% for training cases at the counts predicted 'no' and about 82% for cases with exactly two.

The typical case has the most common value of every attribute (a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1); with a3 = 2 instead, moving a5 away from its first value clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 84%, while with a3 = 1 it stays below 1%.
In the same way, for the typical case with a6 = 2, moving a3 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 75%, while with a6 = 1 it stays below 1%.
Two small parts of the model barely change the predictions.
